findings.claim: The fold's new rule (escaped when an odd run of backslashes precedes $( or a backtick) is the wrong parity for the transport this gate guards. The Bash tool turns each backslash pair into one backslash AFTER the hook reads the command, so bash sees ceil(n/2) backslashes. An opener is literal only when ceil(n/2) is odd, that is when n mod 4 is 1 or 2. n=3 is the fold's new fail-open: the shell runs the gh and MSYS converts its body, yet the row now allows it where 1e36ff59 denied it. n=2 is an over-deny in the other direction. The tests pin only n=1.
findings.counterexample: Hook view, measured: a sed-i deny of a sed expression typed with four backslashes shows provenance matched with four backslashes, so the hook sees the command as written. Bash view, measured under the Bash tool with argv-echo: a single-quoted argument typed with two backslashes arrives with one; echo with two backslashes before $(node …) is a bash parse error showing one backslash before $(, so bash got one; echo with three backslashes before $(node … RAN3) prints RAN3, so it ran; the double-quoted three-backslash form prints Y:/, so it ran and was converted; the three-backslash backtick pair prints Q://, so it ran; the double-quoted two-backslash form prints the substitution as literal text. Shield (probe2 rows 1, 2, 4 and 3): the three-backslash $( form outside quotes, the double-quoted three-backslash form and the three-backslash backtick pair each return allow/no-match on the fold and deny on 1e36ff59; the double-quoted two-backslash form returns deny although nothing runs. Shape of a fix: escaped iff ceil(n/2) is odd; or, fail-closed, escaped only when n=1. Rare shape, but it is a fold regression in the fold's own new predicate.

findings.claim: A backtick body is passed to the recursive scan without bash's backtick unescaping, in which backslash-dollar, backslash-backtick and a backslash pair lose their backslash. The new escape rule then hides a $( that bash runs. Fold-introduced over-allow; the nested escaped-backtick miss and the double-backslash-$( over-deny predate the fold.
findings.counterexample: probe row 38: u=`echo \$(gh pr comment 5 --body /x)` gives new allow, old deny. Measured from m.sh (pure bash) and directly: the same with node argv-echo /x gives X:/. Row 39 (nested escaped backticks): allow on both commits; measured m9 X:/. Row 40 (a backslash pair before $( inside backticks): deny on both; measured m12 is a syntax error, so nothing runs.

findings.claim: blankComments blanks a # after whitespace inside ${ … }, where bash reads the # as word text, not a comment, so a substitution there is hidden. Fold-introduced over-allow.
findings.counterexample: probe row 29: echo ${x:- #$(gh pr comment 5 --body /x)} gives new allow, old deny. Measured with x unset: echo ${x:- #$(node argv-echo /x)} prints #X:/.

findings.claim: blankComments' boundary set omits an operator ). The header (lines 38-40) says a # after a subshell's or a case pattern's ) begins a comment, and tokenizeShell (624-628) reads it that way. So the new comment model disagrees with the module's stated one model of which text is code. The result is an over-deny, which the old row also produced.
findings.counterexample: probe row 24: (true)# $(gh …). probe2 rows 10-11: (cd x)# $(gh …) and case a in a)# $(gh … <LF>;; esac. All deny. Measured: (true)# $(node argv-echo /x) followed by echo after prints only after.

findings.claim: The opt-out state machine around the new flagged push misjudges two set -a / export-by-name orderings. (a) export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV with no value marks the name exported. A later MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 u=$(gh …) therefore reaches gh, but line 937 flags the segment and the row denies. This is a fold-introduced over-deny (the top-level …=1; gh form was already denied). (b) Under set -a, line 932 marks the opt-out exported for the whole statement, but a substitution that comes before the opt-out assignment, or is its value, runs first without it. Over-allow, unchanged from the old commit. (c) Also unchanged from the old commit and not in the header's disclosure: an unset inside the substitution after an outer export.
findings.counterexample: probe2 row 9: export MSYS_NO_PATHCONV; MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 u=$(gh …) gives new deny, old allow; measured m4 prints /x (not converted). probe2 row 6: set -a; u=$(gh …) MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 and probe row 12: set -a; MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=$(gh …) both give allow; measured m2 and m3 print X:/. probe row 13: export …=1; u=$(unset MSYS_NO_PATHCONV; gh …) gives allow; measured m6 prints X:/.

findings.claim: The new glued -bX arm misses pflag's -b=VALUE form. Its value is =/x, which does not start with /, so the row allows it, yet MSYS converts it and gh strips the =.
findings.counterexample: probe row 63: gh pr comment 5 -b=/x gives allow. Measured: argv-echo -b=/x arrives as -b=X:/. gh 2.99.0 accepts gh completion -s=bash the same as -sbash.

findings.claim: The case-insensitive comparison applies only when the name ends in .exe. A bare upper-case GH or Gh runs gh under MSYS bash and is allowed. So is a quoted backslash path without .exe.
findings.counterexample: probe rows 52, 53, 59: GH pr comment 5 --body /x, Gh … and a quoted C:\\tools\\gh … all give allow. Measured: NODE argv-echo /x and Node argv-echo /x both run node and print X:/.

findings.claim: The same defect, solved in two ways: msys-rev-path-subshell still calls msysSegments without the flag. It therefore keeps read 2 F1's defect, in which a prefix-covered or assignment-only segment's $( … ) is dropped although the shell runs it first, without the prefix. It is a warn row.
findings.counterexample: u=$(git show HEAD:a/b) gives warn msys-rev-path-subshell. MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 u=$(git show HEAD:a/b) and MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 echo $(git show HEAD:a/b) both give allow/no-match.

findings.claim: Is the transport's collapse of backslash pairs (measured in F1) charted anywhere? It is not in the module header (grep finds no mention). It reaches past this fold: tokenizeShell resolves a backslash pair as bash would, so a body spelled with two backslashes before /x is read as one backslash and /x, while bash receives one backslash and /x and passes /x. This was the case before the fold too. Is it out of scope for mmnto-ai/totem#2696, or owed as an issue?
findings.counterexample: probe2 row 5: gh pr comment 5 --body with two backslashes before /x gives allow on both commits. Measured: node argv-echo --body with two backslashes before /x arrives as X:/.
